content: 1. Eight additional false positives were identified in molecular WHO-approved rapid diagnostic tests for tuberculosis, with prevalence rates of 5%, 10%, and 20%. These findings are detailed in the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, specifically in Web Annex B, GRADE Summary of Findings Tables 35. 2. Most studies included in the analysis had a low risk of bias, except for one study where the flow and timing were at high risk of bias. Despite this, no downgrading was applied for this factor. 3. Six studies raised concerns regarding applicability. One study focused on pregnant participants, while three studies only included individuals with CD4 cell counts ≤350/μL, which reflects real-world patient presentations. Two studies evaluated only inpatients, where sensitivity estimates were higher and specificity estimates were lower, though specificity remained high (90% and 95%). This discrepancy may be due to the Xpert assay identifying tuberculosis cases that the reference standard (culture) does not. No downgrading was applied for indirectness. 4. Sensitivity estimates across all studies ranged from 25% to 91%. Lower sensitivity was observed in pregnant populations and those on antiretroviral therapy (ART), while higher sensitivity was noted in inpatient studies. However, variability in sensitivity could not always be explained. One level of downgrading was applied for inconsistency. 5. Confidence intervals (CIs) for sensitivity were sufficiently narrow, with a CI half-width of 8. The lower limit was not significantly lower than the lower limit and point estimate of the WHO screen-then-Xpert strategy, while the upper limit was significantly higher. Given the potential for small differences depending on assumed limits and the requirement for Xpert-for-all to have greater or equivalent sensitivity compared to the WHO screen-then-Xpert strategy, no downgrading was applied for imprecision. 6. Specificity estimates ranged from 97% to 100% in all but two inpatient studies, where specificity was 90% and 95%. This variability may be explained by the Xpert assay identifying cases missed by the reference standard. Confidence intervals overlapped, and no downgrading was applied for inconsistency. 7. In studies involving children under five years of age, sensitivity estimates were relatively lower. This may partially explain the differences in sensitivity. One level of downgrading was applied for inconsistency. 8. The number of children with pulmonary tuberculosis contributing to sensitivity analysis was low. The 95% CI around false negatives and true positives could lead to different decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. As inconsistency had already been downgraded, one additional level of downgrading was applied for imprecision. 9. A single study with notably lower specificity used a symptom screen assessing symptoms over the past month, whereas other studies focused on more recent symptoms. This may explain differences in specificity. One level of downgrading was applied for inconsistency. 10. The 95% CI around false positives and true negatives could lead to different decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. One level of downgrading was applied for imprecision. 11. Chest radiography was a component of the composite reference standard in all four studies. One level of downgrading was applied for the risk of bias. 12. One study contributing over 70% of the data was conducted in four countries, one of which is a high tuberculosis burden country. Another study was also conducted in a high tuberculosis burden country. All studies were conducted in outpatient settings. 13. Sensitivity estimates for individual studies ranged from 78% to 100%, with the latter based on only four cases of active tuberculosis. No downgrading was applied for inconsistency. 14. Few patients contributed to the sensitivity analysis. One level of downgrading was applied for imprecision. 15. Specificity estimates for individual studies ranged from 87% to 100%. All three smaller studies had estimated specificity of 100%. No downgrading was applied for inconsistency. 16. Symptom-based screening for tuberculosis in children living with HIV in outpatient settings showed moderate sensitivity and specificity. However, both studies included in the analysis had a high risk of bias in the flow and timing domain, as assessed by QUADAS-2. One level of downgrading was applied for the risk of bias. 17. Specificity estimates for individual studies ranged from 89% to 97%. Differences in clinical diagnosis thresholds may partially explain the observed heterogeneity. One level of downgrading was applied for inconsistency.
